newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-LIPINSKI'S WORLD TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-LIPINSKI'S WORLD TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.

text.p: Since she approached the U.S. National championships five weeks ago, Tara Lipinski's world has been turned upside down.

She entered that event "just to get through it" and won it. Then she took the Champions Series final in Canada and now, at the age of 14 years, nine months and 12 days, she reigns as the youngest women's world figure skating champion in history.
Her Cinderella ride to the top of the tree ended in a third successive triumph over team mate and defending champion Michelle Kwan on Saturday.
But the elfin American's victory was a close thing as she, Kwan and European champion Irina Slutskaya all collected three first place votes from the nine judges for the free skating.
Lipinski, though, could hardly have skated better in her programme of seven triple jumps including the dazzling triple loop-triple loop combination.
"My first three events this season were not good but at the Nationals I began to believe in myself and I was able to carry that through," she said.
She is already working on improvements to her programme which should make her a formidable force at next year's Olympic Games in Japan.
Kwan, meanwhile, was delighted to rediscover the form that had deserted her in her three recent defeats, which followed five successive wins.
Third place went to French girl Vanessa Gusmeroli, a revelation after being sixth in the January's European championships.
There was disaster for the 1995 champion and 1996 runner-up Chen Lu of China, and tragedy for American cover girl and 1995 bronze medallist Nicole Bobek.
Chen missed four month's training with a foot injury and only competed to try and finish in the top 24 for an Olympic qualifying place.
Sadly, she finished 25th and faces a skate-off in October for one of the six remaining Olympic places.
Bobek had to contend with the death of her coach, the highly respected Carlo Fassi, on Thursday, the eve of the event.

"I tried but it was just too hard," Bobek said after slipping from eighth to 13th place on Saturday, despite being supported at rinkside by Fassi's widow Christa and one of his former Olympic champions, Robin Cousins of Britain.
When she finished, she knelt in silent prayer for her coach at centre-ice.
The men's event went for the third time in four years to Elvis Stojko, the tough Canadian for whom no challenge seems too severe.
Fourth after the short programme, he was helped when Russian leader Alexei Urmanov withdrew with a groin injury just before the final six skated.

But Stojko produced his extraordinary quadruple toe loop-triple toe loop combination which earned him a perfect 6.0 from an Italian judge to beat American defending champion Todd Eldredge into second place.
The black-clad Canadian skated to music from the film "Dragonheart".
"It is a story of honour, integrity, strength and power, what I base my skating on," said Stojko, whose artistry is still not everyone's cup of tea.
Unfortunately for Russia, Urmanov's withdrawal meant they will have just two skaters in the Olympic men's event as a result of ill-considered new qualifying rules.

Russia swept all four titles at the European championships but could get only one here, from matchless Olympic champion ice dancers Oksana Gritschuk and Evgeny Platov, winning for the fourth successive year.
The other title, the pairs, went to Mandy Woetzel and Ingo Steuer of Germany.
